text: You get the root of a binary tree and an integer target. Delete every leaf whose value is target. If deleting a leaf turns its parent into a leaf, and the parent also has value target, delete the parent too. Keep going until you can't. Return the new root.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — a node is deleted only when it's a leaf and its value is target. An inner node with value target stays, unless all of its children get deleted first. Then it becomes a leaf, and it can go too. Is that right?
Yes. That chain reaction is the whole point.

Okay. So the real question is order. Whether a node is a leaf depends on what happened to its children, so I should finish the children first, and only then decide about the parent. And if the root itself gets deleted, I return null. An empty tree is a valid answer, right?
Right. That's example three: one, two, null, two, null, two with target two gives just one, and if the root were also a two, you'd return an empty tree.
Are there any constraints on the input size?
Between one and three thousand nodes. Values and target are between one and a thousand.

Got it. The tree can be a straight chain, so the depth can reach three thousand. I'll remember that for recursion. Let me run through the example: one, two, three, two, null, two, four, with target two. D and E are leaves with value two, so they go. Once D is gone, B has no children, so B is now a leaf with value two, and B goes too. That's the chain reaction. C keeps the four, so C stays. The answer is one, null, three, null, four, which matches.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would copy the rule word for word: scan the whole tree, delete every target leaf, and repeat until a scan deletes nothing. It's correct, but a long chain of targets needs a fresh scan for every level, so that's quadratic work. This problem reminds me of post-order DFS — the pattern for when a parent's answer depends on its children's final answers. I clean the left subtree, clean the right subtree, and then look at the node. By then its children are final, so the chain reaction happens for free, in one pass.

Here's the plan. One: null returns null. Two: clean both children and write the results back into left and right — a child that comes back null was deleted. Three: if the node is now a leaf with the target value, return null; otherwise return the node. One thing worth flagging — the order is a correctness requirement, not a style choice. Take one, null, one with target one. Pre-order checks the root while it still has a child, keeps it, deletes the child, and never looks at the root again. It returns one instead of an empty tree — and it fails thirty-seven thousand seven hundred seventy exhaustive cases. There's a trade-off here: an explicit stack is safer for very deep trees, but three thousand levels is fine, and recursion is easier to check. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. Base case first. Then I clean both children and assign the results back. The last line asks one question: is this node a leaf now, and is it the target? If yes, return null; if not, return the node. One thing worth flagging — that assignment back is not optional. If I call the recursion and throw away the result, the parent still points to the deleted child, so one, null, one stays unchanged. And the leaf test needs and, not or. With or, a node with only one child counts as a leaf, so one, null, two with target one returns an empty tree, losing a child that should stay.

Let's dry-run the code on example one, target two, expecting one, null, three, null, four. The row that matters is B. In the input, B is not a leaf — it has D. But by the time we check B, D has already come back null, so B is a leaf with value two, and it goes — the chain reaction in a single pass. Corner cases: example two drops both leaf threes but keeps the middle three, which still has the two. Example three's chain of twos collapses to just one. One, null, one with target one returns an empty tree — the pre-order trap. One, null, two with target one stays whole — the or trap. Against a slow repeat-until-nothing-changes simulation, there were zero mismatches.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear: each node is visited once, and each null child is one quick call — exactly two n plus one calls, so six thousand and one for three thousand nodes. Space is the tree height, just the call stack. In the worst case the tree is a straight chain, three thousand and one calls deep, and that runs fine; a balanced tree is only thirteen calls deep. For something like a million nodes, I'd switch to the explicit stack. Oh, one more thing — my code cuts deleted nodes out but never frees them. On an all-target chain that's three thousand leaked nodes. LeetCode accepts that, but in production C plus plus I'd delete the node right before returning null, or use smart pointers.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You saw early that the problem is really about order, and you picked post-order because a node's leaf status depends on its children being final — so the cascade needs no second pass. You showed pre-order is a correctness bug, not a speed issue, with the tiny counterexample one, null, one. And you flagged that assigning the results back, and and versus or, each break the answer — plus the memory leak a real codebase would care about. Good work.
